title: sed and awk
goal: Edit config files with sed, cut out parts of logs, and compute counts, sums and averages with awk.
setup: # P1/P5/P7: a Spring Boot style config
# P2: a deploy log with sections

printf '%s\n' '# deploy log' '09:00 checking cluster' '=== deploy start ===' '09:01 pull image todo-api:2.4.1' '09:02 apply manifests' '09:03 rollout status: ok' '=== deploy end ===' '09:04 cleanup' '# end of file' > deploy.log
# P3: access log: ip method path status bytes ms
# P5: users file and a broken script

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# 1) Print app.conf with the log path /var/log/todo changed to /data/logs/todo (no edit)' '# 2) Print name and role (columns 1 and 3) of each user in users.csv (comma separated), no header' 'OLD=/var/log/todo' 'NEW=/data/logs/todo' 'sed "s/$OLD/$NEW/" app.conf' 'awk "{print $1, $3}" users.csv' > report.sh

warmup.q: Which grep options print only the matching part with extended regex?
How do you remove comment and empty lines from a config with grep?

warmup.a: `return` gives only an exit code 0-255; 8080 becomes 144. Use `echo 8080` and `PORT=$(get_port)`.

warmup.q: What does `"$@"` do in a wrapper script?
warmup.a: It passes every argument on, exactly as given, also arguments with spaces.

problems.title: sed: change config values safely
problems.situation: The to-do API moves to a new database server and a new port. The user must change `app.conf` without opening an editor (a CI job will do the same). First print the result, then edit the file with a backup, then check the change with `diff`.
task: Print the file with `server.port` changed from 8080 to 9090 (no edit yet).
Print it with every `db01.internal` changed to `db02.internal`.
Change the log path `/var/log/todo` to `/data/logs/todo`. Use `|` as the delimiter, because the path has `/`.
Now edit the file for real with all three changes in one `sed -i.bak` command (with `-e` for each change).
Show what changed with `diff app.conf.bak app.conf`.
hints: Basic form: `sed 's/old/new/' file`. Add `g` at the end to change every match on a line.
Any character can be the delimiter: `sed 's|/var/log/todo|/data/logs/todo|'`.
`-i.bak` edits the file and keeps the old version as `app.conf.bak`.
solution: diff app.conf.bak app.conf; echo "diff exit code: $? (1 = files differ)"

explanation.meaning: Substitute: replace the first match on each line.
Global: replace every match on the line, not only the first.
Anchors: match the whole line, so `server.port=80800` is not changed.
Escape the dot. In regex `.` means any character.
Another delimiter, so slashes in paths need no escaping.
Edit in place and save the original as `.bak`. Without `-i`, sed only prints.
Several edits in one run. `\` at the end of a line continues the command.
`diff` returns 1 when the files are different (Day 2). Here that is the expected result.

problems.expected_output:
server.port=9090
db.url=jdbc:postgresql://db02.internal:5432/todo
log.path=/data/logs/todo/app.log
2,3c2,3
< server.port=8080
< db.url=jdbc:postgresql://db01.internal:5432/todo
---
> server.port=9090
> db.url=jdbc:postgresql://db02.internal:5432/todo
5c5
< log.path=/var/log/todo/app.log
---
> log.path=/data/logs/todo/app.log
diff exit code: 1 (1 = files differ)
mistakes: Slashes in the pattern: `sed "s/$OLD/$NEW/"` with a path gives `sed: -e expression #1, char 9: unknown option to` and the letter `s`. Use `|` as delimiter.
`sed -i` with no backup on the only copy of a config. One wrong regex and the file is broken. Use `-i.bak` or test without `-i` first.
`sed 's/old/new/' file > file` empties the file: bash truncates it before sed reads it.

checks.run: cp app.conf c.conf; sed 's/a/b/' c.conf > c.conf; wc -c < c.conf

problems.interview_say: I first run sed without `-i` to see the result, then use `sed -i.bak` so I have a backup, and check with `diff`. For paths I use `|` as the delimiter.
problems.try_yourself: Use a variable: `PORT=7070; sed "s/^server.port=.*/server.port=$PORT/" app.conf | grep port`. Why double quotes here?

problems.title: sed: print and delete lines and ranges
problems.situation: The release manager wants only the deploy part of `deploy.log` (from `=== deploy start ===` to `=== deploy end ===`) for the release notes, without comment lines.
task: Print only lines 2 to 4 with `sed -n '2,4p'`.
Delete comment lines with `sed '/^#/d'`.
Print the block from `deploy start` to `deploy end` with a range of two patterns.
Print the same block, but without the two `===` marker lines.
Delete the first and the last line of the file (`1d` and `$d`).
hints: `-n` = print nothing unless told. `p` = print. `d` = delete.
A range is `start,end`. Both can be line numbers or `/patterns/`.
For the inner block: pipe the result into `sed '1d;$d'`.
solution: echo "=== without first and last line ==="

explanation.meaning: Print only lines 2, 3 and 4.
Delete every line that starts with `#`.
Print from the first line that matches `start` to the next line that matches `end`.
Delete line 1 and the last line. `$` here means the last line, and `;` separates two commands.

09:01 pull image todo-api:2.4.1
=== no comments ===
09:00 checking cluster
=== deploy start ===
09:01 pull image todo-api:2.4.1
09:02 apply manifests

=== deploy end ===

=== deploy start ===

mistakes: Forgetting `-n` with `p`: every line is printed, and the matching lines are printed twice.
Using double quotes around `'1d;$d'`: bash replaces `$d` with an empty variable, and sed gets `1d;`.
problems.interview_say: `sed -n 'X,Yp'` prints a range of lines, and `/start/,/end/p` prints a block between two patterns. `d` deletes lines, for example `sed '/^#/d'` removes comments.
problems.try_yourself: Print the file with line numbers using `sed =`. Then try `sed -n '$='` to count the lines.

problems.title: awk: a response time report
problems.situation: The team lead asks: "How many requests failed, what was the average response time, and which requests were slow?" The access log has 6 fields: ip, method, path, status, bytes, ms. awk splits each line into fields `$1` to `$NF`.
task: Print the IP and the status of each line (`$1`, `$4`).
Print the line number (`NR`) and the number of fields (`NF`) of each line.
Print only requests with status 500 or more (`$4 >= 500`).
Count requests and compute the average time (`$6`) in `END`.
Print a header in `BEGIN` and a nicely formatted summary with `printf`.
hints: `awk '{print $1, $4}' access.log`. A comma between fields prints a space.
A condition before the braces: `awk '$4 >= 500 {print}' file`.
`{ sum += $6; n++ } END { printf "avg %.1f ms\n", sum / n }`.
solution: END { printf "requests: %d, errors: %d, avg: %.1f ms\n", n, err, sum / n }' access.log

explanation.meaning: Fields of the line, split by spaces. `$0` is the whole line.
Number of the Record (line) / Number of Fields on this line.
Pattern and action: run the action only for lines where the pattern is true.
Variables start at 0. Add up the time and count the lines.
Run once before the first line / once after the last line.
Formatted print: text left in 14 spaces, number right in 6, decimal with 1 digit.

mistakes: Double quotes around awk code: `awk "{print $1}"` lets bash replace `$1` first. Always use single quotes.
Dividing in `END` when the file is empty: Ubuntu's default awk (mawk) prints `-nan`, and gawk stops with `division by zero attempted`. Check `if (n > 0)` first.
Comparing as text: if a field is `-` or has letters, awk compares it as a string and the result is strange.
problems.interview_say: awk splits each line into fields. I use `$1`, `NR` and `NF`, conditions like `$4 >= 500`, and `END` to print sums and averages, for example `awk '{s+=$6} END {print s/NR}'`.
problems.try_yourself: Print the slowest request only: `sort -k6 -n access.log | tail -n 1`, then do the same with awk using a `max` variable.

problems.title: awk on a CSV: cost per service
problems.situation: Finance sent the cloud cost export `billing.csv`. The user must report the total cost per service (EC2, S3, RDS) and the grand total. The file is comma separated and has a header line.
task: Print the service and cost columns with `-F,` (skip the header with `NR > 1`).
Sum the cost per service in an awk array: `sum[$2] += $3`.
Print each service and its total in `END`, sorted by name.
Print the grand total with 2 decimals.
hints: `-F,` sets the field separator to a comma.
awk arrays work like bash associative arrays: `sum["EC2"]`.
`for (s in sum)` has no fixed order; pipe the output into `sort`.
solution: END { for (s in sum) printf "%-4s %6.2f\n", s, sum[s] }' billing.csv | sort
awk -F, 'NR > 1 { t += $3 } END { printf "%.2f USD\n", t }' billing.csv

explanation.meaning: Split fields at commas instead of spaces.
Skip line 1 (the header).
An array keyed by service name; add the cost to that key.
Loop over all keys in END.
awk gives keys in random order. Sort for a stable report.

problems.expected_output:
EC2 12.50
S3 1.20
EC2 12.50
RDS 8.00
S3 1.30
EC2 13.00
=== total per service ===
EC2   38.00
RDS    8.00
S3     2.50
=== grand total ===
48.50 USD
mistakes: No `-F,`: the whole line is `$1`, so `$2` and `$3` are empty and all sums are 0.
Not skipping the header: `cost` is added as 0, and `service` appears as a key in the report.
CSV with quoted commas (`"Smith, John"`) breaks `-F,`. For real CSV files, use a proper tool (Python, `csvkit`).
problems.interview_say: For a quick CSV report I use `awk -F,` with `NR > 1` to skip the header and an array like `sum[$2] += $3` to group values, then sort the output.
problems.try_yourself: Add the number of rows per service: `cnt[$2]++`, and print `service total count`.

problems.title: Find the bug: the sed and awk report
problems.situation: `report.sh` should print `app.conf` with a new log path, and the name and role of every user. sed fails with a strange error, and awk stops with a syntax error.
task: Run `bash report.sh` and read the errors and the output.
Find 4 bugs: the sed delimiter, the awk quotes, the field separator, and the header.
Fix them. The sed output must show `log.path=/data/logs/todo/app.log`, and awk must print 3 lines: `pasindu associate`, `nimal senior`, `kavya lead`.
hints: The variables contain `/`, which ends the `s/.../.../` early. Use `|`.
awk code in double quotes: bash replaces `$1` and `$3` (empty) before awk starts.
Add `-F,` and the condition `NR > 1`. Pass shell values to awk with `-v` if needed.
solution: # 1) Print app.conf with the log path /var/log/todo changed to /data/logs/todo (no edit)
# 2) Print name and role (columns 1 and 3) of each user in users.csv (comma separated), no header

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: with `/` as delimiter, the `/` inside `/var/log/todo` ended the pattern. Double quotes are right here, so bash puts the variables in.
Bug 2: in double quotes, bash replaced `$1` and `$3` with empty text, so awk got `{print , }`: `syntax error at or near ,`. Single quotes keep `$1` for awk.
Bug 3: the file is comma separated.
Bug 4: skip the header line.

problems.expected_output:
sed: -e expression #1, char 8: unknown option to `s'
awk: line 1: syntax error at or near ,
--- fixed ---
log.path=/data/logs/todo/app.log
pasindu associate
nimal senior
kavya lead
mistakes: Changing sed to single quotes too: then `$OLD` is not replaced and nothing matches. sed needs double quotes here; awk needs single quotes.
To use a shell variable in awk, write `awk -v role="$ROLE" '$3 == role'`, not `$ROLE` inside the awk code.
problems.interview_say: Two classic traps: slashes in sed patterns (use another delimiter) and double quotes around awk code (use single quotes and pass shell values with `-v`).
problems.try_yourself: Print only users with the role `lead` using `-v`: `awk -F, -v r=lead '$3 == r {print $1}' users.csv`.

problems.title: awk tricks: $NF, line counts, column checks
problems.situation: Small awk one-liners save time in daily work: the last field of each line, counting lines, finding broken lines with the wrong number of columns, and unique values.
task: Print the last field of each line in `access.log` with `$NF`.
Count the lines: `awk 'END {print NR}'`.
Find lines in `billing.csv` that do not have exactly 3 fields.
Print each IP only once, in the order seen: `awk '!seen[$1]++'`.
hints: `$NF` = the field number NF = the last field.
With `-F,` the separator is a comma: `NF != 3`.
`!seen[$1]++` is true only the first time a key appears.
solution: awk -F, 'NF != 3 {print "bad line " NR ": " $0}' billing.csv; echo "(no output = all lines have 3 fields)"

explanation.meaning: Last field. `$(NF-1)` is the one before it.
After the last line, NR is the line count (like `wc -l`).
Lines with a different number of columns, often broken data.
Print the first time each value appears. Like `sort -u`, but keeps the order.

problems.expected_output:
35
120
2300
6 lines
(no output = all lines have 3 fields)
10.0.0.5
10.0.0.7
192.168.1.20
mistakes: Writing `$NF-1` for the second to last field: awk computes (last field) minus 1. Write `$(NF-1)`.
problems.interview_say: `$NF` gives the last field, `NR` the line number, and `!seen[$1]++` removes duplicates but keeps the original order.
problems.try_yourself: Print the number of fields of every line in `deploy.log`. Which lines have the most words?

problems.title: sed with groups: mask secrets, reformat dates
problems.situation: Before sending a config to a vendor, the user must hide the password. A report also needs dates as `DD/MM/YYYY` instead of `YYYY-MM-DD`. sed capture groups `( )` with `\1` keep parts of the match.
task: Print `app.conf` with the value after `db.password=` replaced by `*****`.
Convert `2026-10-01` to `01/10/2026` in the dates of `billing.csv` (print only the first 3 lines).
hints: `sed -E 's/(db.password=).*/\1*****/'`: `\1` is the text of the first group.
Dates: `([0-9]{4})-([0-9]{2})-([0-9]{2})` and `\3/\2/\1`. Use `|` as delimiter because the new text has `/`.
`-E` allows `( )` and `{4}` without backslashes.

explanation.meaning: A group: remember this part of the match.
Put the remembered groups back, in any order.
Any text until the end of the line (the secret).
Extended regex for sed (like `grep -E`).

mistakes: Masking with `grep -v password` removes the line. The vendor then does not know the setting exists. Masking keeps the key.
Never paste real secrets in tickets or chat, even masked. Rotate a secret if it was shown by mistake.
problems.interview_say: I use sed groups to keep part of a match, for example `s/(password=).*/\1*****/` to mask secrets before I share a config or a log.
problems.try_yourself: Mask every number in the `db.url` port: `sed -E 's/:[0-9]+\//:****\//' app.conf | grep db.url`.

interview.q: How do you replace a word in a file without opening an editor?
interview.a: `sed -i.bak 's/old/new/g' file`. `-i` edits in place, `.bak` keeps a backup, `g` changes every match on a line.

interview.q: How do you print only lines 10 to 20 of a file?
How do you print the first column of a file with awk? And for a CSV?
How do you compute the average of a column with awk?
Why do we use single quotes around awk programs?
interview.a: So bash does not replace `$1`, `$2` and so on. Those are awk fields, not shell variables.

recap.meaning: Replace text (g = all matches on a line)
Edit in place with a backup
Print a block between two patterns
Line number / field count / last field

recap.example: awk -F, '{s[$2]+=$3} END {for(k in s) print k, s[k]}'

recap.meaning: Pass a shell value into awk
